newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Historians meet to launch Swiss World War Two probe.
newsitem.headline: Historians meet to launch Swiss World War Two probe.

text.p: A powerful commission of independent historians met for the first time on Wednesday to lay a strategy for a sweeping probe of neutral Switzerland's controversial financial ties to Nazi Germany.

The five Swiss and four foreign experts were meeting in Berne until March 8 after being hastily picked by the Swiss government in December to answer a hail of international criticism that Switzerland profited from World War Two.

The commission is empowered by a federal decree to lift bank secrecy laws on historical records as well as look into otherwise confidential government files, powers Berne has never before granted to an expert enquiry.

"Today is more of an informal introductory session because one of the foreign members is not ariving until tonight and another is coming tomorrow," said Linus von Castelnur, chief of staff of the panel's secretariat.

The group, known as the Bergier commission after its chairman Jean-Francois Bergier, is due to devote its inaugural session to drafting a strategy and settling practical matters such as hiring a team of 20 or so researchers.

The commission, which has a mandate of five years but expects to report at least every six months on its progress, is one link in a major Swiss effort to repair the country's tarnished international image after months of bitter argument with Jewish critics.

Swiss President Arnold Koller took another step on Wednesday by proposing the creation of a huge humanitarian fund that would use Swiss official gold reserves to aid victims of human rights abuses, catastrophes and the Holocaust.

Other parts of the effort include a fund for rapid humanitarian aid to impoverished Holocaust survivors set up last month with 100 million Swiss francs ($67.3 million) from the country's three big global banks.

The big Swiss banks and Berne are acting after months of bitter criticism led by the World Jewish Congress, which says banks hoarded accounts left by Holocaust victims and that Switzerland as a whole profited cynically from the war.
Bergier's commission is expected to deliver two reports to the cabinet in the next few months on Swiss central bank purchases of Nazi gold and on Berne's wartime policy of rejecting Jewish refugees.
Then researchers can begin their broader task of charting the size and flow of waves of assets sent to the neutral banking nation for wartime safety, for sale or for transfer to the wider world.

The commission's foreign members are former Polish foreign minister Wladyslaw Bartoszewski, Israeli historian Saul Friedlaender, Princeton University professor Harold James and Sybil Milton, a senior historian at the Holocaust Museum in Washington D.C.

The Bergier commission is separate from a panel chaired by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker set up last May by Swiss banks and the WJC to sweep Swiss bank records for accounts left by victims of Nazi genocide. ($ = 1.485 Swiss Francs)
